title: A Letter to the Exiles: Settle Down and Seek the City's Peace
summary: Jeremiah sends a letter to the Judeans deported to Babylon in 597 BC. He tells them to build houses, plant gardens, raise families, and pray for the welfare of Babylon, because the exile will last seventy years; only then will God bring them home, according to his plans to give them a future and a hope. The letter warns against prophets in Babylon who promise a quick return, names two of them for judgment, and ends with a rebuke of Shemaiah, who wrote back demanding that Jeremiah be silenced.
story: This chapter completes the set of three (27 to 29) about false hopes in Zedekiah's early years. Chapter 24 had called the exiles the good figs; now Jeremiah tells them how to live as good figs in a foreign land. His message runs against every instinct of a displaced people: don't keep your bags packed, settle in; don't curse your captors' city, pray for it. It also carries the first extended word of hope in the book's second half. The promise that God will bring them back after seventy years leads directly into the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33), with its vision of restoration and a new covenant.
historical:
The letter was sent some time after the deportation of 597 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar took King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), the queen mother (Nehushta, 2 Kings 24:8), court officials, and skilled workers to Babylon. It traveled with an official delegation from King Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar, perhaps connected with the tensions of 594 or 593 BC seen in chapters 27 and 28, when Zedekiah may have needed to reassure his overlord. One courier, Elasah son of Shaphan, belonged to the family that protected Jeremiah (26:24). The other, Gemariah son of Hilkiah, is otherwise unknown; whether his father was the high priest Hilkiah of Josiah's reign is uncertain.

The exiles were not scattered as slaves. Many were settled in communities of their own in the Babylonian countryside, such as Tel-abib by the Chebar canal where Ezekiel lived (Ezekiel 3:15). Cuneiform business records from a village called Al-Yahudu (literally Judah-town), dating from the sixth and fifth centuries BC, show Judean families there leasing land, paying taxes, and giving their children names that honored the LORD. Jeremiah's instructions describe the kind of life those records reveal.
cultural:
Building a house, planting a garden or vineyard, and marrying a wife were the three basic acts of settling down in Israel's world; Deuteronomy 20:5-7 exempts a man from war if he has just done any of them. Jeremiah deliberately uses that vocabulary to tell the exiles to put down roots. The command to have children and multiply echoes God's first blessing on humanity (Genesis 1:28) and his promise to Abraham: even in Babylon, the people of God are to grow, not shrink.

Praying for a foreign city was startling. Israel's psalms of exile could be bitter against Babylon (Psalm 137). Jeremiah asks the exiles to seek Babylon's shalom, its peace and well-being, because their own shalom is bound up with it. Verse 22 contains a grim pun: Hebrew for “curse” (qelalah) sounds like the verb for roasting (qalah), used for the two prophets Nebuchadnezzar burned to death. Burning was a Babylonian penalty (compare Daniel 3), and their crime was probably political: prophecies of Babylon's quick fall would sound like sedition.
literary: The chapter preserves an actual letter and a follow-up exchange. Verses 1 to 3 are a narrative heading, verses 4 to 23 give the letter itself, and verses 24 to 32 report Shemaiah's counter-letter, quoted inside Jeremiah's reply. The letter moves from instruction (settle, marry, pray, verses 4 to 7), to warning (don't trust the prophets, 8 and 9), to promise (seventy years, then return, 10 to 14), to judgment on those left in Jerusalem and on two false prophets (15 to 23). The word shalom anchors the central section: the exiles are to seek the city's shalom (verse 7), and God's plans for them are plans of shalom (verse 11, rendered “to prosper you”). Verses 16 to 20 are missing from the Greek translation and may have been added to the letter when the book was compiled; they reuse the rotten figs of chapter 24.

outline.t: Build, plant, marry, and pray for Babylon; ignore false prophets
After seventy years: a future and a hope
Judgment on those who remain in Jerusalem
Ahab and Zedekiah, the lying prophets
Shemaiah's letter and the LORD's verdict on him

doctrines.note: God says he himself sent the exiles to Babylon (verses 4, 7, 14). Their displacement was not outside his plan, and ordinary life there (houses, gardens, marriages) could be lived faithfully under his care.
The hope God offers is real but long. It does not deny the seventy years; it lies on the far side of them. Biblical hope is confidence in God's promised future, not a guarantee of relief this year.
God's people are told to seek the good of the city where they live as outsiders and to pray for it. Their well-being is tied to the well-being of their neighbors, even their captors.

Verses 12 to 14 promise that when the people call and seek God with all their heart, he will be found. The return from exile is linked to a renewal of prayer and wholehearted seeking, as Daniel 9 later illustrates.

words.note: Shalom, peace, but much more than the absence of war: wholeness, well-being, prosperity, things being as they should be. It appears in verse 7 (three times in Hebrew, rendered “prosperity” and “prospers”) and verse 11. The exiles' shalom is bound up with Babylon's.

Machashavah, a plan, thought, or intention. It can be used of evil schemes (18:18, the plots against Jeremiah) or of God's purposes. In verse 11 God's plans are plans of shalom for his people as a whole, worked out over seventy years.

Darash, to seek, inquire, or care about. The exiles are to seek the city's welfare (verse 7) and will search for God with all their heart (verse 13, alongside a second verb for seeking). The same word is used for consulting God through a prophet, so seeking God himself is set against seeking a quick word from false prophets.

Golah, the exile or the community of exiles. It names the deported people as a group, which is the audience of this letter. Every “you” in verses 10 to 14 is plural in Hebrew and addressed to this community.

christ: The New Testament takes up the exiles' situation as a picture of the church's life in the world. Peter addresses believers as exiles and sojourners and urges them to live honorably among the nations (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11-12), much as Jeremiah told the exiles to build, plant, and seek the city's good. Paul urges prayers for kings and all in authority so that believers may live peaceful and quiet lives (1 Timothy 2:1-2). The promise of return after exile belongs to the larger hope the prophets held out, of God gathering his scattered people, which the Gospels see beginning in Jesus, who came to gather the lost sheep of Israel and then the nations. The promise of verses 13 and 14, that those who seek God with all their heart will find him, is echoed in Jesus' words that those who seek will find (Matthew 7:7-8), though Jesus does not quote this verse. These are thematic links: the chapter's own promise concerns Judah's return from Babylon.

hard.q: Can I claim Jeremiah 29:11 as a personal promise that God will prosper me and not harm me?
hard.a:
Start with its first readers. The promise was given to the Judean community in exile in Babylon, and the “you” is plural throughout. It came with a hard condition of time: it would be fulfilled only after seventy years (verse 10), which meant that most adults who first heard the letter would die in Babylon. The plans “to prosper you and not to harm you” were God's plans for the people's future as a whole, brought home under Cyrus decades later, not a promise that each reader's circumstances would improve soon. In fact the letter was written specifically to rebut prophets who promised quick relief.

That does not make the verse irrelevant to Christians. It reveals God's character: he has purposes of shalom for his people, he keeps his promises across generations, and he is found by those who seek him with all their heart. Christians rightly take comfort from that, since the New Testament says God's promises find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). The misreading is to treat the verse as a guarantee of personal success or of a problem solved soon. Read in context, it offers something sturdier: hope that holds even when the exile is long and you may not see its end yourself.

questions: Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens in a place they did not want to be. What would it look like for you to invest fully in a season of life you did not choose?
Why do you think God asked the exiles to pray for Babylon's peace? Whose welfare would you find hard to pray for?
How does knowing that Jeremiah 29:11 was spoken to a community facing seventy years of exile change the way you hear its promise?
